questiontext.text: What is a struct used for?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A struct gathers related data under one name, so a student's name and score can travel together as a single object.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: Grouping variables of different types into one new type

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Point {
    int x;
    int y;
};

int main() {
    Point a = {1, 2};
    Point b = a;
    b.x = 7;
    cout << a.x << " " << b.x << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Point b = a; makes an independent copy. Changing b.x does not touch a, so a.x stays 1 while b.x is 7.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

int main() {

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Braces fill the members in order, and every member that is not mentioned is zeroed. So x is 7 and y is 0.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Counter {
    int hits;
};

void a(Counter c) {
    c.hits += 5;
}

void b(Counter& c) {
    c.hits += 2;
}

int main() {
    Counter k{1};
    a(k);
    b(k);
    cout << k.hits << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. Function a receives a copy, so its +5 is lost. Function b receives a reference, so its +2 changes the original: 1 + 2 = 3.

questiontext.text:
Match each term with its meaning.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Struct  →  [[1]]

Member  →  [[2]]

Object  →  [[3]]

Constructor  →  [[4]]

Comparator  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. These five words describe the whole life of a struct: define it, create objects, and put them in order.

The correct answer:

  • Struct → A new type that groups several members
  • Member → A variable or function inside the struct
  • Object → A variable made from the struct type
  • Constructor → A function that runs when an object is created
  • Comparator → A rule that tells sort which element comes first

Sort each statement: does it compile? (struct Point { int x; int y; }; Point p = {1, 2}; is declared above)

Drag the correct label next to every item.

cout << p.x;  →  [[1]]

cout << p.z;  →  [[2]]

p.y = 5;  →  [[1]]

cout << p;  →  [[2]]

Point q = p;  →  [[1]]

p.x();  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. Members are reached by name, so a missing member is an error. A struct cannot be printed with << unless you write that operator yourself, and x is a number, not a function. These statements were all tested with a real compiler.

The correct answer:

Compiles: cout << p.x;, p.y = 5;, Point q = p;
Does not compile: cout << p.z;, cout << p;, p.x();

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct Item {
    string name;
    int price;
};

int main() {
    vector<Item> v = {{"pen", 3}, {"ink", 1}, {"cap", 3}};
    sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const Item& a, const Item& b) {
        if (a.price != b.price) {
            return a.price < b.price;
        }
        return a.name < b.name;
    });
    for (const Item& it : v) {
        cout << it.name << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The cheapest item (ink, price 1) comes first. The other two cost 3, so the name breaks the tie alphabetically: cap before pen.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <set>
using namespace std;

struct Event {
    int start;
    int end;
    bool operator<(const Event& other) const {
        return end < other.end;
    }
};

int main() {
    set<Event> s;
    s.insert({1, 5});
    s.insert({2, 5});
    s.insert({3, 6});
    cout << s.size() << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The set compares events with operator<, which looks only at the end time. {1, 5} and {2, 5} have the same end, so neither is smaller and the set treats them as one element.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;

struct Rect {
    int w;
    int h;
    Rect(int w_, int h_) : w(w_), h(h_) {}
    int area() const { return w * h; }
    int perimeter() const { return 2 * (w + h); }
};

int main() {
    Rect r(3, 4);
    cout << r.area() << " " << r.perimeter() << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The constructor stores w = 3 and h = 4. The area is 3 x 4 = 12, and the perimeter is 2 x (3 + 4) = 14.

name.text: Q14 - Drag and drop - fill the gaps

questiontext.text:
Drag the correct pieces into the gaps so the points are sorted by x in descending order (the program should print 9 5 2).

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct P {
    int x;
    int y;
};

int main() {
    vector<P> v = {{2, 0}, {9, 0}, {5, 0}};
    sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const P& a, const P& b) {
        return a.[[1]] [[2]] b.x;
    });
    for (const P& p : v) {
        cout << p.x << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. To put larger values first the rule says "a comes before b when a.x is greater than b.x". Using < would give ascending order.

The correct answer:

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct P {
    int x;
    int y;
};

int main() {
    vector<P> v = {{2, 0}, {9, 0}, {5, 0}};
    sort(v.begin(), v.end(), [](const P& a, const P& b) {
        return a.x > b.x;
    });
    for (const P& p : v) {
        cout << p.x << " ";
    }
    cout << endl;
    return 0;
}

questiontext.text:
Match each declaration with what it means.

Drag each description onto the item it belongs to.

Point q = p;  →  [[1]]

Point& q = p;  →  [[2]]

const Point& q = p;  →  [[3]]

p.x  →  [[4]]

Point p{};  →  [[5]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. The ampersand decides whether we copy or alias, and const decides whether we may change.

The correct answer:

  • Point q = p; → An independent copy of p
  • Point& q = p; → Another name for p itself
  • const Point& q = p; → A read-only alias, no copy
  • p.x → The member x of the object p
  • Point p{}; → An object with every member zeroed

questiontext.text: Why is return a.score <= b.score; a bad comparison rule for sort?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A comparison rule must return false for equal elements. A rule that is true for equal elements breaks the assumptions of sort and can cause crashes or endless loops.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: It is not strict: for equal elements it says each comes before the other, which can crash sort
It is slower but always correct

Sort each function: is the parameter passed by value (a copy) or by reference?

Drag the correct label next to every item.

void f(Point& p)  →  [[2]]

generalfeedback.text:
Explanation. No ampersand means the function receives a copy. An ampersand, with or without const, means it works on the original object.

The correct answer:

By value (copy): void f(Point p), void f(Point q, int k), void h(Student s)
By reference: void f(Point& p), void f(const Point& p), int g(const Student& s)

questiontext.text: When is a struct a better choice than a pair?

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. A pair gives only first and second. A struct lets you write name and score, and it can hold as many members as you need.

incorrectfeedback.text: Not quite. Read the explanation below.

answer.text: When you want meaningful member names or more than two members
When you need the fastest possible code
When you want to avoid headers

questiontext.text:
What does this program print?

main.cpp
#include <iostream>
#include <string>
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

struct S {
    string name;
    int score;
};

int main() {
    vector<S> v = {{"A", 3}, {"B", 9}, {"C", 9}};
    S best = v[0];
    for (const S& s : v) {
        if (s.score > best.score) {
            best = s;
        }
    }
    cout << best.name << endl;
    return 0;
}

generalfeedback.text: Explanation. The loop replaces best only when a score is strictly greater. B (9) beats A (3), but C (9) is not greater than 9, so B stays.
